concepts.description: The accident model an investigator holds determines what counts as a cause, what evidence is gathered, and which countermeasures look reasonable — so the model must be chosen consciously, not inherited by default.
concepts.title: Your Accident Model Shapes What You Find

concepts.description: The claim that some workers are inherently accident-prone rests on the method-of-percentages fallacy — statistics that ignore unequal exposure to risk — and was statistically discredited by the 1940s–50s.
concepts.title: The Accident-Proneness Myth

concepts.description: A complex adaptive system cannot be simultaneously fully optimised for its current environment and resilient to a changed one — tight tuning to "what is" is bought with brittleness against "what might become."
concepts.title: Adapted versus Adaptive — The Optimality/Brittleness Trade-Off

concepts.description: What makes systems safe changes with how safe they already are — and beyond about one failure in a million, more rules add nothing, while practical drift becomes the dominant residual risk.
concepts.title: Amalberti's Safety Continuum and the Ultra-Safe Plateau

concepts.description: Weak, ambiguous danger signals are evaluated through an organisation's operating mindset — a standardized, compliance-driven culture dismisses them as known issues, where an experimental culture treats each as a hypothesis to test.
concepts.title: Ambiguous Threats and the Standardized vs Experimental Mindset

concepts.description: Mindful organizations treat unfamiliar events as anomalies worth investigating; mindless ones relabel them as normal, concealing information that foreshadows trouble.
concepts.title: Anomalizing Versus Normalizing

concepts.description: Weick and Sutcliffe's split of HRO mindfulness into three anticipation principles that slow escalation of weak signals and two containment principles that limit damage once surprise has begun.
concepts.title: Anticipation Versus Containment

concepts.description: Eight organisational practices that protect the unreported vulnerable spots of an ultra-safe system, from meta-monitoring and structural dissent to measuring the work-as-imagined/work-as-done gap.
concepts.title: Armor Strategies Against Drift in Ultra-Safe Operations

concepts.description: Two structural ways a control system's parts fall out of sync with each other — overlapping control zones producing ambiguous or conflicting authority, and one subsystem changing without a corresponding update to the controllers and assumptions built around it.
concepts.title: Asynchronous Evolution and Boundary Overlaps

concepts.description: Because no account of a complex-system failure can be an objective mirror of what "really" happened, judge an account by whether it authentically conveys the insiders' lived experience, and deliberately keep multiple such accounts alive rather than converging on one official story.
concepts.title: Authenticity Over Accuracy in Failure Accounts

concepts.description: It is unfair and analytically wrong to hold practitioners accountable for outcomes they lacked the authority or resources to control — especially after the organisation itself demanded the efficiency trade-off.
concepts.title: The Authority–Responsibility Mismatch

concepts.description: A three-way split of how a macro-level property relates to its micro-level parts — nominal (directly derivable), weak (derivable only by running the full system), and strong (not derivable even in principle) — that sharpens the general resultant-vs-emergent distinction into a workable taxonomy.
concepts.title: Bedau's Taxonomy of Emergence

concepts.description: BBS programmes apply 1930s behaviorism — observe, reward, sanction worker acts — re-enshrining the unsafe-acts myth and measurably suppressing injury reporting through fear, incentives, and stigma.
concepts.title: Behavior-Based Safety and Its Failure Modes

concepts.description: Punishing individuals after failure teaches everyone else to hide mistakes, cutting off the information flow that safety learning depends on — without removing a single error trap.
concepts.title: Blame Suppresses Reporting and Learning

concepts.description: A deliberate, acknowledged operating regime that keeps a system running outside its formally updated rules because full compliance is economically or physically infeasible — distinct from normalisation of deviance because the gap is named and managed rather than eroding unnoticed.
concepts.title: Borderline Tolerated Conditions of Use

concepts.description: Situations anticipated in advance, however unlikely, stay inside a system's envelope of potential variability; situations no one envisaged at all are qualitatively different, and resilience depends on recognising which kind is currently underway.
concepts.title: The Boundary of Potential Variability

concepts.description: People occupying a position in a system reliably adopt that position's characteristic, locally rational view of the world — which is why blaming the individual who currently holds the role rarely improves outcomes and redesigning the system usually does.
concepts.title: Bounded Rationality and Role Perspective

concepts.description: A risk diagram centred on a single loss-of-control event, with threat detection and avoidance on one side and recovery, mitigation, and containment on the other — used to show that resilience spans both directions, not just post-event recovery.
concepts.title: The Bowtie Model of Resilience

concepts.description: An unexpected event as an abrupt test of structures built before chaos arrives — where every unprepared weakness becomes a complex problem at once.
concepts.title: Brutal Audit

concepts.description: Four structural properties — buffering capacity, flexibility, margin, and tolerance — that distinguish a resilient system from a brittle one under the same disruption.
concepts.title: Buffering Capacity, Margin, and Tolerance

concepts.description: Two training-shaped failure patterns — mental models that are wrong (buggy) and knowledge that is correct but fails to activate in real operational context (inert).
concepts.title: Buggy and Inert Knowledge

concepts.description: The oldest accident model treats failure as a linear domino sequence triggered by a weakest link — usually a human unsafe act — and buys its simplicity with severe analytic sacrifices.
concepts.title: Chain-of-Events Accident Model

concepts.description: Actively summing several individually-tolerable risk factors into a cumulative judgment of shrinking margin, rather than checking each factor separately against its own limit, is a distinct and not automatically triggered skill.
concepts.title: Choke-Point Detection

concepts.description: The stance high-reliability organisations use to resist drift — treating past success as no guarantee of future safety, welcoming doubt and minority views, and keeping leadership close enough to the sharp end to hear bad news.
concepts.title: Chronic Unease

concepts.description: Under dynamic fault management, operators either settle on one plausible hypothesis that shields itself from contrary evidence or jump between explanations with every new cue — and only hindsight says which was wrong.
concepts.title: Cognitive Fixation and Thematic Vagabonding

concepts.description: Dutch and EU railway safety data show that ultra-high safety and organisational resilience are independent attributes — a rigid, centralised "stop and restart" regime achieves ultra-safe outcomes with none of resilience's characteristic flexibility, at the cost of everything flexibility would have bought.
concepts.title: Command-and-Control as an Alternative to Resilience

concepts.description: The fourth HRO principle: investing in general capabilities to detect, contain, and recover from errors that have already occurred rather than assuming prevention alone will suffice.
concepts.title: Commitment to Resilience

concepts.description: Under genuine complexity, centralised command breaks down; pushing decision authority to the periphery only works safely if paired with an explicit, mandatory mechanism that forces cross-boundary communication.
concepts.title: Communication Forcing Functions for Distributed Authority

concepts.description: Two popular investigation labels that restate the outcome as if it were a cause — an abstract construct cannot cause events, and both labels collapse under circularity.
concepts.title: Complacency and Loss of Situation Awareness Are Pseudo-Explanations

concepts.description: A complicated system (many parts, but exhaustively describable by its designer) turns complex (not exhaustively describable even in principle) the moment it is released into an open, changing operating environment.
concepts.title: Complicated Systems Become Complex Once Fielded

concepts.description: Letting analysts follow up with a reporter before de-identifying their submission captures far richer safety detail than fully anonymous reporting — a design choice distinct from, and often confused with, protecting reporters from blame.
concepts.title: Confidentiality Without Anonymity in Reporting Systems

concepts.description: Expectations function as hypotheses that steer attention toward confirming evidence and away from disconfirming cues — creating blind spots that let small errors incubate until a brutal audit.
concepts.title: Confirmation-Seeking in Expectations

concepts.description: Weick and Sutcliffe's nine recurring self-assessment questionnaires that probe mindful infrastructure before a crisis — the deliberate counterpart to the abrupt test a brutal audit applies after one.
concepts.title: Conscious Mindfulness Audits

concepts.description: System resilience rests on coordinating distributed action across vertical, lateral, and longitudinal axes, and the tools built for routine coordination are exactly what strain or break first under crisis conditions.
concepts.title: Coordination Dimensions of Resilience

concepts.description: Explanations of the form "they should have / failed to / if only they had" describe a utopian world that never existed and explain nothing about why people actually did what they did.
concepts.title: Counterfactual Reasoning in Investigations

concepts.description: Wreathall and Jones's five prioritised criteria for choosing a proactive safety indicator — objective, quantitative, available, worthy, compatible — grounded in a spectrum from formal models to expert-brainstormed factors.
concepts.title: Criteria for Selecting Safety Indicators

concepts.description: Acceptance of resilience-engineering ideas over traditional safety assumptions varies systematically by national and occupational culture, and practitioners hold both paradigms simultaneously and inconsistently rather than committing to one — so RE cannot be rolled out as a one-size-fits-all message.
concepts.title: Cultural Variation in Resilience Uptake

concepts.description: When hierarchy, status, or fear makes people literally unable to speak up about physical danger, the resulting silence — not the original hazard — becomes the proximate cause of catastrophe.
concepts.title: Dangerous Silence in High-Risk Systems

concepts.description: Information being physically present in the system is not the same as information being perceivable by the operator given displays, workload, lighting, and attentional focus.
concepts.title: Data Availability vs Data Observability

concepts.description: Successfully reducing a hazard's frequency over years leaves the active workforce with no personal experience of it, because the people who remember it firsthand have been promoted away from day-to-day operations — a demographic mechanism distinct from ordinary complacency.
concepts.title: Decay of Hazard Awareness Through Workforce Turnover

concepts.description: A two-phase failure signature in which visible stability conceals a control mechanism working harder and harder to mask a growing disturbance, until its capacity is exhausted and the masked parameter collapses suddenly.
concepts.title: Decompensation — Exhausting the Capacity to Adapt

concepts.description: Three ways investigators strip behaviour of its unfolding context — micro-matching against procedures, cherry-picking quotes to fit a label, and shopping-bagging scattered cues into one clear warning.
concepts.title: Decontextualization Traps

concepts.description: Drift proceeds through steps small enough that each one is beneath the threshold of remark, so the slide is structurally invisible to the people living through it, not merely psychologically overlooked.
concepts.title: Decrementalism

concepts.description: The fifth HRO principle: during non-routine problems, authority migrates to whoever holds the most relevant knowledge rather than whoever holds rank.
concepts.title: Deference to Expertise

concepts.description: Reviewers discount a precursor incident's relevance by fixating on surface-level differences from their own context — location, personnel, equipment version — concluding "it couldn't happen here" while missing the deeper structural pattern the two events actually share.
concepts.title: Distancing Through Differencing

concepts.description: A wider repertoire of perspectives and possible responses (requisite variety) is the strongest available lever against drift, but it has to be built deliberately by managing how influence is weighted, not just how many people are in the room.
concepts.title: Diversity as a Safety Resource

concepts.description: Accidents incubate as small, individually rational departures from design assumptions accumulate over long periods, gradually eroding safety margins while everything appears to be going fine.
concepts.title: Drift into Failure

concepts.description: Reliable, safe performance looks like nothing happening because constant mutual adjustment among operators compensates for changing conditions — masking the mindful work that produces stability.
concepts.title: Dynamic Non-Event

concepts.description: Resilience redefined for a systemic accident model — not resisting disturbance but reacting early enough that recovery stays local, because damping caught the deviation before it grew large enough to spread.
concepts.title: Dynamic Stability, Damping, and Confined Recovery

concepts.description: Systems under competitive pressure tend to settle at the point of maximal adaptability just short of turbulent breakdown, where small perturbations usually produce small responses but can, rarely and unforeseeably, trigger a disproportionate one.
concepts.title: Optimised at the Edge of Chaos

concepts.description: Hollnagel's principle that being maximally efficient and maximally thorough at the same time is not a solvable problem, so every operator and manager is continuously trading one against the other, usually invisibly.
concepts.title: The Efficiency–Thoroughness Trade-Off (ETTO)

concepts.description: A checklist for auditing whether an organisation is actually resilient, as distinct from merely currently safe — each criterion names a specific way resilience is absent even where accident rates look fine.
concepts.title: Woods's Eight Criteria of Organisational Resilience

concepts.description: A resultant property is predictable directly from its parts; an emergent one is not — and accidents in complex sociotechnical systems are emergent, which is why an organisation with zero individually error-prone people can still produce a catastrophic organisational accident.
concepts.title: Emergence — Resultant vs Emergent Phenomena

concepts.description: Design features that make a system robust against expected anomalies are not the same thing as resilience — resilience additionally requires deliberately harnessing human adaptive capability, which is itself a double-edged asset that must be tuned, not just permitted.
concepts.title: Engineered Robustness versus Controlled Resilience

concepts.description: How much an investigator can actually learn from an accident depends on their distance from it along a spectrum from emotionally overwhelmed proximity to sterile, decontextualised remoteness — with a "second stories" sweet spot in between that neither extreme reaches.
concepts.title: Epistemic Distance and the Sweet Spot for Organisational Learning

concepts.description: Reason's distinction between organisational culture (slow-moving, organisation-wide) and local workplace climate (fast-changing, shaped by immediate leadership and conditions) — a site can sit inside a strong overall safety culture while its local climate is acutely error-likely.
concepts.title: Error-Likely Climate vs Safety Culture

concepts.description: A formally defined dynamic process — an initial irregularity spreading across operational areas at accelerating tempo, generating consequences that are hard to overview and impossible to predict in advance.
concepts.title: Escalation

concepts.description: Experienced practitioners often detect danger not by recognising a familiar threat pattern but by noticing that events are failing to match what a recognised situation should produce next — which is why the warning is so hard for them to articulate.
concepts.title: Expectancy Violation as Anomaly Detection

concepts.description: Explaining why a past event happened and finding the levers that prevent the next one are different analytic products — the best change factor is often not among the explanatory factors at all.
concepts.title: Explanatory Factors vs Change Factors

concepts.description: The mistaken belief that because one occupies a central, important role one must already know what others see — which stops subordinates from passing information upward and leaves the central figure less informed than assumed.
concepts.title: Fallacy of Centrality

concepts.description: The four standard post-incident fixes — reprimand, retrain, new procedure, more automation — treat systemic vulnerabilities as isolated defects and leave the conditions for the next event intact.
concepts.title: The Fallacy of the Quick Fix

concepts.description: Justifying a design decision by pointing to a similar-looking predecessor system is only valid if the analogue matches on the causally relevant dimension, not merely on surface features — a mismatch on the dimension that actually matters produces confident, systematic under-investment.
concepts.title: False Analogue Transfer in Safety-Critical Design

concepts.description: Fatigue degrades vigilance, reasoning, and — critically — the ability to assess one's own impairment; the effective countermeasures are roster and sleep-opportunity design, not slogans.
concepts.title: Fatigue as a Systemic Condition

concepts.description: A time gap between a risk-increasing cause and its visible effect does more than slow the response — it generates false confidence while risk accumulates unseen, and can push a correction, once it finally arrives, to overshoot.
concepts.title: Feedback Delay Masks Accumulating Risk

concepts.description: Whether reactive incident reporting can actually work in a given domain is set by five structural characteristics of that domain, not by how well the reporting programme itself is designed — and where they're absent, the fix is a different kind of system, not a better version of the same one.
concepts.title: Five Structural Dimensions of Incident Reporting Viability

concepts.description: Under STAMP, every controller — human or automated — acts on an internal model of the system's current state, and accidents occur specifically when that model diverges from the system's actual state without the controller knowing it has diverged.
concepts.title: Flawed Process Models in Control-Theoretic Accidents

concepts.description: Anticipation, monitoring, response, and learning — the four abilities a system must exercise continuously to stay in control, each one's absence producing a distinct, named failure mode.
concepts.title: The Four Abilities of Resilient Performance

concepts.description: Human activities settle into one of four governance archetypes — each with its own primary safety tool and its own diminishing-returns limit — so the safety tool that works for one archetype does nothing, or actively harms, in another.
concepts.title: Amalberti's Four Archetypes of System Resilience

concepts.description: Managing a transition between organisational functional states requires recognising the trigger, having a defined transition routine, having the receiving state actually ready to operate, and being able to rebound back — and the 2004 Swedish Foreign Department response to the Sumatra tsunami shows what happens when the first requirement fails.
concepts.title: Four Requirements for State-Transition Resilience

concepts.description: Model a system as coupled functions rather than coupled components, so that catastrophic outcomes can be traced to the normal, everyday performance variability of several functions combining — not to any single function breaking.
concepts.title: Functional Resonance Analysis Method (FRAM)

concepts.description: The specific real-time cognitive capacities that let a team move from the shock of a genuinely unanticipated event into effective action — distinct from the capacities that handle anticipated abnormal situations.
concepts.title: Responding to Fundamental Surprise

concepts.description: A person explaining away one piece of disconfirming evidence at a time can drift arbitrarily far from the correct understanding of a situation without any single step feeling like a red flag — the individual-cognition mirror of organisational normalisation of deviance.
concepts.title: Garden Path Fallacy and Snap-Back

concepts.description: Four team-level, non-domain-specific competencies — information management, communication and coordination, decision-making, and effect control — that let a team keep functioning once role-specific procedures stop applying.
concepts.title: Generic Competencies for Escalating Situations

concepts.description: Incident classification schemes routinely conflate surface manifestations of an event with the underlying causal patterns that produced it, which corrupts both signal detection and trend analysis.
concepts.title: Genotype vs Phenotype in Incident Categorization

concepts.description: A system-level failure of adaptation — strategies that succeeded repeatedly become rigid and keep being applied even as accumulating evidence shows the environment has shifted past their design assumptions.
concepts.title: Getting Stuck in Outdated Behaviours

concepts.description: A componential investigation digs deeper into the failing subsystem's own parts; a systemic one steps outward into the organisational, historical, and political context that put those parts under pressure in the first place.
concepts.title: Investigate Up and Out, Not Down and In

concepts.description: Organisations pursue efficiency, cost, and safety simultaneously; management passes the irreconcilable trade-offs down for sharp-end operators to negotiate locally, which is where "violations" and drift originate.
concepts.title: Goal Conflicts and Production Pressure

concepts.description: A feedback loop faithfully optimises whatever it is actually told to optimise; a safety metric that is easy to measure but is not the same thing as safety produces exactly that metric, not safety.
concepts.title: Goal Displacement in Safety Metrics

concepts.description: Organisational rules operate at three distinct specification levels — goal, process, and action — and a gap at the goal level forces frontline operators to improvise the strategic judgement no one above them supplied.
concepts.title: Goal, Process, and Action Rules

concepts.description: The claim that minor incidents and fatalities occur in a fixed ratio is refuted — in safe complex systems minor incidents and catastrophes have different causal mechanisms, so low injury counts do not predict disaster.
concepts.title: The Heinrich Triangle Myth

concepts.description: Empirical theory of how organisations (air traffic control, aircraft carriers, power plants) sustain consistently safe operation despite complexity, and its central blind spot around expert judgment under uncertainty.
concepts.title: High-Reliability Organization (HRO) Theory

concepts.description: Knowing the outcome makes an event look far more predictable and preventable than it was, collapsing the uncertain branching situation people actually faced into a simple linear story of choosing to err.
concepts.title: Hindsight Bias

concepts.description: How much time and predictability an actor has determines which of four qualitatively different control modes they operate in — strategic, tactical, opportunistic, or scrambled — and each mode change downgrades planning horizon and effectiveness together, not independently.
concepts.title: Hollnagel's Four Control Modes (COCOM)

concepts.description: Labelling something "human error" marks where investigation should start, not where it may stop — the error points to deeper trouble in tools, tasks, and organisation.
concepts.title: Human Error Is a Symptom, Not a Cause

concepts.description: Klein's four-stage protocol for eliciting what participants actually experienced — unassisted story first, then read-back, joint juncture identification, and probing — because memory is malleable and leading cues corrupt it.
concepts.title: Human-Factors Debriefing

concepts.description: A recovered incident is simultaneously evidence a system successfully stretched to absorb disruption and evidence of how close it came to a fracture point — the same episode supports both readings at once.
concepts.title: Incidents Are Ambiguous Markers of Adaptive Capacity

concepts.description: A safety programme that succeeds at driving accidents toward zero destroys its own traditional source of safety information in the process, and must build a deliberate alternative before that happens.
concepts.title: The Information Paradox of High-Safety Systems

concepts.description: James Reason's model of a safety culture where managers and operators hold current knowledge of human, technical, organizational, and environmental factors — sustained by four interlocking subcultures.
concepts.title: Informed Culture

concepts.description: The same blunt-end effort to pre-determine every response and eliminate operational variability erodes the sharp-end improvisational skill that becomes the system's only resource once an event falls outside what was pre-determined.
concepts.title: The Irony of Resilience

concepts.description: Evaluative vocabulary — "complacency", "inattention", "misdiagnosis", "failure to" — judges performance after the fact in place of explaining it, and should be purged from findings.
concepts.title: Judgmental Language

concepts.description: How an organisation responds to practitioners involved in failure: retributive schemes sort people into culpability bins after the fact, while restorative just culture centres account-giving, repair, and forward-looking accountability.
concepts.title: Just Culture — Retributive vs Restorative

concepts.description: Every system is operated at the limit of its current capacity, so any gain from a technological or organisational improvement gets consumed by increased tempo, scope, or complexity rather than banked as slack.
concepts.title: The Law of Stretched Systems

concepts.description: Whether a given metric counts as leading or lagging is not a fixed property of the metric — it depends on which control level is using it and over what response timescale, so the same number can be lagging locally and leading systemically at once.
concepts.title: Leading and Lagging Indicators Are Level-Relative

concepts.description: What people did made sense to them at the time given their goals, attention, knowledge, and constraints — so the investigative question is why it made sense, not what they failed to do.
concepts.title: The Local Rationality Principle

concepts.description: Static rule-based limits and performance-based, actively managed risk assessment are two different ways of achieving safety, and the shift from one to the other requires regulators to change what they evaluate, not just relax the rules.
concepts.title: Managed Safety vs Regulated Safety

concepts.description: A socio-technical system's core technology-to-task coupling has a finite lifespan running through four predictable phases, ending in a collapse that resets the system to a lower safety baseline rather than a smooth continuation of improvement.
concepts.title: The Master-Coupling-Paradigm Life Cycle

concepts.description: As a situation departs further from what was anticipated, the useful response shifts from concrete, action-level protocols toward abstract, goal-level guidance — a fixed procedure is only well-matched to low uncertainty.
concepts.title: Matching Response Abstraction to Uncertainty

concepts.description: Three techniques for making a manager's real safety-versus-production priority visible and comparable, because self-report from the manager alone is the least reliable of the three.
concepts.title: Measuring Managerial Safety Commitment

concepts.description: Resilience engineering's leverage is not predicting the next accident or bolting on more external controls, but making an organisation sensitive to whether the risk model it is already using is still valid — control of the control of risk.
concepts.title: Meta-Control of Risk

concepts.description: A self-report survey administered to one operational function measures that function's individual operational capabilities, not the system-level anticipation/monitoring/response/learning cornerstones — because those cornerstones depend on cross-functional feedback loops no single survey population can see or report on.
concepts.title: Micro-Survey Factors Diverge from Macro Resilience Cornerstones

concepts.description: Organisational resilience at the managerial level depends on middle managers actively buffering top-down production pressure from senior leadership against the safety needs of the workforce — a role that fails through either failing to notice the threat or noticing it and failing to act on it.
concepts.title: Middle Managers as the Safety Buffer Against Executive Production Pressure

concepts.description: In HROs under pressure, decisions move up and down the hierarchy to wherever the person with the most event-specific knowledge happens to be, decoupling authority from rank.
concepts.title: Migrating Decisions

concepts.description: Weick and Sutcliffe's term for rich awareness of discriminatory detail — the cognitive infrastructure enacted through the five HRO principles that lets organizations notice weak signals before they become brutal audits.
concepts.title: Mindfulness in High-Reliability Organizing

concepts.description: A compact nine-item validated questionnaire that proxies the full mindfulness-audit battery — units scoring higher report fewer medication errors and patient falls in hospital nursing research.
concepts.title: Mindfulness Organizing Scale

concepts.description: A safety intervention that protects one population can increase net harm if it pushes activity onto a substitute that carries a higher baseline risk — protecting the visible group can cost the displaced group more than it saves.
concepts.title: The Modal Risk-Trading Paradox

concepts.description: A proactive monitoring architecture needs more than one cadence — routine continuous tracking, time-bound probes, change-triggered checks, and indicator-triggered deep dives each catch a different kind of risk shift.
concepts.title: Four Monitoring Cadence Modes

concepts.description: The cluster of features — time pressure, high stakes, ill-defined goals, missing information, and dynamic change — that define real sharp-end decisions and explain why they cannot be judged against laboratory-style rational-choice standards.
concepts.title: Naturalistic Decision-Making Conditions

concepts.description: The inherited worldview that systems decompose into parts connected by traceable, proportional cause-effect links — adequate for simple systems, and the reason chain-of-events and root-cause reasoning feel self-evident even when they mislead.
concepts.title: Newtonian-Cartesian Accident Thinking

concepts.description: Pariès's mapping of Bedau's first two emergence classes onto organizational resilience — resilience computable from designed individual and collective traits (nominal) versus resilience arising from feedback and self-organisation that only the running system itself produces (weak).
concepts.title: Nominally and Weakly Emergent Resilience

concepts.description: Vaughan's mechanism by which incremental nonconformity becomes the accepted local norm, because each small rule departure is rewarded immediately and punished only eventually, if ever.
concepts.title: Normalization of Deviance

concepts.description: The foundational contrast between treating human error as the cause of failure in otherwise-safe systems (Bad Apple theory) and treating it as a symptom of deeper systemic trouble in systems that are not inherently safe.
concepts.title: Old View vs New View of Human Error

concepts.description: Any psychological label in a finding must be decomposed into observable components with a documented path from data to conclusion — otherwise it is a judgment pasted over the data.
concepts.title: Leaving an Analytic Trace — Operationalizing Labels

concepts.description: Woods and Wreathall's analogy from ductile-metal mechanics — an organisation absorbs and recovers from stress up to a yield point, beyond which cognitive overload produces spiking errors and permanent (non-recoverable) capability loss, not just slower recovery.
concepts.title: The Organizational Stress-Strain Model

concepts.description: Training a team's generic escalation competencies in a domain unrelated to their real work strips away the ego and prestige stakes that make trainees defend familiar procedures instead of reflecting on how they actually handled the unexpected.
concepts.title: Out-of-Domain Simulation for Resilience Training

concepts.description: Judging the quality of a decision by the severity of its outcome rather than by the information available when it was made — including the illusion that bad outcomes must have had bad processes behind them.
concepts.title: Outcome Bias

concepts.description: Retold workplace stories quietly teach newcomers what is actually acceptable to do — pushing back on a superior, refusing reassurance, asking for help — communicating the organisation's real norms more effectively than any written policy.
concepts.title: Permission Stories

concepts.description: Reducing accidents and worker harm depends on encouraging people to report hazards and concerns — interpersonal safety to speak up precedes and enables physical safety interventions, not the reverse.
concepts.title: Physical Safety Requires a Speak-Up Culture

concepts.description: Deliberately probing for early physical and behavioural indicators that a project's risk profile is shifting, and the organisational-design lesson that this only works when done by people embedded in the work, not by off-site specialists monitoring from a distance.
concepts.title: Pinging: Proactive Probing for Risk-Profile Shifts

concepts.description: Sticking with the original plan as conditions gradually deteriorate, because strong early cues supported it and later contrary cues arrive weak, ambiguous, and incremental.
concepts.title: Plan-Continuation Bias

concepts.description: Coordinating interdependent units through many overlapping, locally responsive centres of control rather than one central authority or fully independent local units — the structural answer to working at cross-purposes.
concepts.title: Polycentric Control Architectures

concepts.description: Ask a team to imagine the plan has already failed and explain why, rather than asking them to critique the plan directly — reframing scrutiny as a creativity challenge breaks the overconfidence that vested authors bring to reviewing their own plan.
concepts.title: The Premortem Technique

concepts.description: The first HRO anticipation principle: treating any lapse, near miss, or weak signal as a possible symptom of deeper system trouble rather than as noise to be smoothed over after success.
concepts.title: Preoccupation with Failure

concepts.description: Resilient decision-making under escalating uncertainty optimises not for the current moment alone but for keeping enough adaptive capacity in reserve to handle whatever comes next — avoiding irreversible commitments while the situation is still unfolding.
concepts.title: Preserving Margin for Future Response

concepts.description: Classical safety control only updates policy after an outcome fails; proactive monitoring inserts intermediate process and environmental indicators directly into the feedback loop so control action can happen before the outcome is compromised.
concepts.title: Proactive Monitoring as a Control-Loop Redesign

concepts.description: The incremental, locally rewarded departure of actual practice from written procedure, driven by overdesigned rules, production goals, and invisible safety margins.
concepts.title: Procedural Drift

concepts.description: The New View of procedures — not the safest prescribed way to work but flexible resources whose safe application is itself a complex cognitive skill, resting on design assumptions real work routinely violates.
concepts.title: Procedures as Resources for Action

concepts.description: Regulators, auditors, and internal risk functions are embedded in the same web of local pressures as the operation they oversee, so they can actively contribute to drift rather than merely fail to catch it.
concepts.title: Protective Structures Can Fuel Drift

concepts.description: Emergency procedures and trained reflexes only work when interpersonal risk does not crowd out speaking, listening, and acting on them — psychological safety is a precondition for protocol use, not a substitute for it.
concepts.title: Protocols Require a Speak-Up Culture

concepts.description: Every operation is squeezed between an economic boundary, a workload boundary, and a safety boundary, and management/competitive pressure systematically pushes it toward the latter two.
concepts.title: Rasmussen's Three-Boundary Model

concepts.description: The dominant post-1970s accident narrative that treats decision-makers as fully-informed utility-optimisers, so a bad-looking outcome must mean they were insufficiently informed, careless, or corrupt — the theoretical engine behind Bad Apple theory.
concepts.title: The Rational-Choice (Amoral-Calculator) Explanation of Failure

concepts.description: Experienced practitioners under time pressure do not compare options — they recognise a situation as an instance of a familiar pattern, which supplies a workable action directly, and check that action with mental simulation rather than against alternatives.
concepts.title: Recognition-Primed Decision (RPD) Model

concepts.description: Fixing a component-level vulnerability by adding a barrier, checker, or redundant layer creates new relationships between parts, and that relationship growth can make the system less safe even as each part individually becomes more reliable.
concepts.title: Added Barriers Can Increase Complexity Risk

concepts.description: A three-tier typology of threats by how much prior pattern exists to respond from — routine, one-off but conceivable, and beyond anyone's collective experience — because each tier calls for a structurally different kind of preparedness, not just "more" of the same readiness.
concepts.title: Regular, Irregular, and Unexampled Threats

concepts.description: The second HRO anticipation principle: holding categories, labels, and diagnoses loosely so heterogeneous details that foreshadow trouble are not lost when impressions are named for coordination.
concepts.title: Reluctance to Simplify

concepts.description: Organisational resilience is not a fixed safety margin a system either has or lacks — it is a set of ongoing capabilities to recognise, steer away from, and recover from the edges of safe operation.
concepts.title: Resilience as Adaptive Capacity, Not a Static Property

concepts.description: A system is "in control" to the extent it can minimise unwanted performance variability in itself and its environment — and loss of control traces to one of four specific constraints, not a single generic cause.
concepts.title: Resilience as a Form of Control

concepts.description: Raw accident counts and rates say nothing about resilience on their own — a system can look dangerous only because it has enormous exposure, or safe only because it rarely encounters the hazard at all, so any resilience comparison must first normalise for how often the hazard was actually encountered.
concepts.title: Risk Exposure Normalization

concepts.description: A system tends to drift back toward its habitual level of risk acceptance even after an intervention adds safety margin, because the same efficiency pressure that consumed the margin before is still present afterward.
concepts.title: Risk Homeostasis

concepts.description: When the language used to describe a recurring anomaly quietly shifts toward a less alarming category, that shift is itself worth monitoring as a signal, regardless of whether any specific bad outcome can be predicted from it.
concepts.title: Risk Relabelling as a Leading Indicator

concepts.description: Complex system failures have no single root cause — contributing factors are individually necessary and only jointly sufficient, and any "root cause" is just the arbitrary point where an investigation stopped.
concepts.title: The Root-Cause Fallacy

concepts.description: Explicit decisions to relax production pressure to stay clear of a safety boundary; the real test of a safety culture is how it treats a sacrifice that, in hindsight, turned out not to have been necessary.
concepts.title: Sacrifice Judgements and the True Test of Safety Culture

concepts.description: Under extreme time and information pressure, decision-making shifts from Simon's ordinary satisficing to deliberately abandoning the highest-payoff option in order to cap the worst-case downside — not the same thing as a proactive sacrifice judgement made before a crisis exists.
concepts.title: Sacrificing Decisions Under Crisis

concepts.description: The accumulation of safety paperwork, compliance processes, and metrics that does not touch real operational risk — and actively harms safety by suppressing information, eroding expertise, and producing fantasy documents.
concepts.title: Safety Bureaucracy and Safety Clutter

concepts.description: Modelling safety as keeping performance variability within an acceptable boundary reframes monitoring around two symmetric force sets — what pushes variation out of control and what pulls it back — and traditional safety practice only ever tracked the first.
concepts.title: Safety as a Control Problem — Upward and Downward Forces

concepts.description: The interpretivist view treats culture as emerging from daily interactions and influenceable only through them, against the functionalist view of culture as an attitude-object management can own, measure, and campaign into shape.
concepts.title: Safety Culture Is Something an Organization Does, Not Has

concepts.description: Safety is created and destroyed on the line; a safety function isolated as arms-length staff degenerates into metric tabulation and liability management unless deliberately re-grounded in operations.
concepts.title: The Safety-Department Staff Trap

concepts.description: Hollnagel's paradigm contrast — safety as the absence of negative events versus safety as the presence of capacities to succeed under varying conditions — which flips what to study and how to treat human variability.
concepts.title: Safety-I and Safety-II

concepts.description: Training scenarios that deliberately reproduce escalation's real dynamics — cascading, cross-boundary, unfolding over time — and specifically bait the cognitive traps a team needs practice resisting, rather than rehearsing a single well-defined problem to a known procedure.
concepts.title: Scenario Design for Escalation Training

concepts.description: As an organisation gets better at solving problems it must lower its threshold for what counts as a problem, or learning stalls exactly when the remaining risks become invisible.
concepts.title: Seeking Ever-Weaker Failure Signals

concepts.description: Letting one actor control both the execution of a risky action and the verification that reports on it removes the independent feedback a control loop depends on, so the single point of control can distort or suppress the very data that would reveal its own drift.
concepts.title: Segregation of Duties as a Control Barrier

concepts.description: A small, seemingly inconsequential early classification or design decision can cascade through a complex system's history and determine major downstream safety consequences decades later.
concepts.title: Sensitive Dependence on Initial Conditions (in Accident Causation)

concepts.description: The third HRO anticipation principle: staying attentive to the messy reality of frontline work — what people are actually doing, not what plans say they should do.
concepts.title: Sensitivity to Operations

concepts.description: A second, independently-derived checklist for auditing organisational resilience — top-level commitment, just culture, learning culture, awareness, preparedness, flexibility, and opacity — synthesised from roughly 65 organisational safety models.
concepts.title: Seven Core Themes of Resilient Organizations

concepts.description: Practitioners in direct contact with the safety-critical process (sharp end) work inside constraints created by the organisational layers above (blunt end) — and reactions to failure are biased toward blaming the sharp end.
concepts.title: Sharp End and Blunt End

concepts.description: Distributed practitioners each handling an unfolding situation as a fresh, local event — without projecting beyond the immediate window to integrate history or anticipate trajectory — can trap the whole system in a local minimum even though every individual response looks reasonable.
concepts.title: Sharp-End Myopia

concepts.description: Failing to act on a weak signal is not always a failure to notice it — an organisation can perceive a diffuse anomaly perfectly well and still fail at the separate, structurally distinct step of translating that perception into a recognised, escalatable safety issue.
concepts.title: The Signal Perception vs Translation Gap

concepts.description: A three-way taxonomy of problem types — simple, complicated, complex — used to explain why a technique that works for one kind of problem (a recipe, a checklist) fails or even backfires on another.
concepts.title: Simple, Complicated, and Complex Problems (Zimmerman & Glouberman)

concepts.description: Every complex adaptive system is well-adapted, under-adapted, and maladapted all at once, in different respects — which is why a linear causal model cannot predict how it will behave under a new disruption.
concepts.title: The Simultaneous Triple-State Theorem

concepts.description: How long a system takes to recover from routine disturbances is itself a leading indicator — recovery getting slower means adaptive capacity is being consumed, even while every individual disturbance still gets handled.
concepts.title: Slowing Recovery Time as a Tipping-Point Signal

concepts.description: HRO principles are raised through concrete, complete outcomes of moderate importance — opportunistic cumulative changes at controllable sites, not by shutting the organization down or decomposing one big redesign into steps.
concepts.title: Small Wins for Mindful Organizing

concepts.description: Adding human checking layers does not stack reliability the way redundant components do — human checkers are interdependent, so double-checking can increase error rates instead of reducing them.
concepts.title: The Social Redundancy Fallacy

concepts.description: The ethical stance of fatal-accident investigation — reconstructing why actions made local sense, rather than reducing the deceased to a list of failures — protects both the dead and the operators who face the same traps tomorrow.
concepts.title: Speaking for the Dead

concepts.description: Case studies conducted on the actual ground where an event happened, putting participants in decision-makers' shoes with HRO principles as an interpretive lens — vicarious learning without tactical fault-finding.
concepts.title: Staff Rides for Safety Learning

concepts.description: Leveson's STAMP models a sociotechnical system as two parallel control hierarchies (development and operations) linked by a downward reference channel and an upward measuring channel — and shows how severing the upward channel blinds the higher levels even while operations continue.
concepts.title: STAMP's Hierarchical Control Structure

concepts.description: Organisational resilience requires continuously managing five concrete trade-offs between standardizing tendencies (procedure, audit, routine automation) and flexibility tendencies (local autonomy, informal practice, learning) — none of which resolves once and stays resolved.
concepts.title: The Standardization-versus-Flexibility Organizational Tension

concepts.description: Following Ashby's cybernetics, an organisation's operation decomposes into a small set of recognisable functional states — from normal functioning through disturbed functioning to decay — with transition rules between them that are sometimes irreversible or require passing through an intermediate state.
concepts.title: State-Space Model of Organizational Functioning

concepts.description: Managing the unexpected requires amplifying response to small, ambiguous clues — the opposite of the normal instinct to treat weak signals with weak action until they become visible crises.
concepts.title: Strong Response to Weak Signals

concepts.description: Resilience properties like organisational culture that cannot be reduced to individual traits even in principle, because the system's beliefs about its own future causally alter its present behaviour — which makes a functioning safety culture structurally a self-defeating prophecy.
concepts.title: Strongly Emergent Resilience and the Self-Defeating Prophecy

concepts.description: Formal management-system audits and informal safety-culture assessments measure different halves of organisational resilience and neither substitutes for the other — audits anchor resilience in structure that outlasts any one team, but are structurally blind to exactly the criteria culture assessment exists to catch.
concepts.title: Structural Audits vs Culture Assessment for Resilience

concepts.description: FMEA, event trees, and fault trees all assume fixed structural relationships between components, which makes them blind to the dynamic couplings and simultaneous ordinary-event interactions that produce accidents in complex systems.
concepts.title: Structural Limits of Tree-Based Risk Assessment

concepts.description: Separate units each drift their local practice away from shared formal procedure in mutually invisible ways, and the divergence only becomes dangerous when an unplanned tightly-coupled moment forces the never-reconciled practices to combine.
concepts.title: Structural Secrecy and Cross-Unit Practical Drift

concepts.description: The proactive practice of learning how daily work actually succeeds — six field questions and an engagement posture — because pre-catastrophic risk lives in unreported routine adaptations, not in incident data.
concepts.title: Studying Normal Work

concepts.description: Sharp-end practitioners quietly withhold resources from management's view specifically to preserve reserve capacity for sudden demand surges, compensating for margin that top-down efficiency drives keep consuming.
concepts.title: Subversive Investments in Slack

concepts.description: Reason's model of accidents as a hazard trajectory passing through holes in layered defences, distinguishing sharp-end active failures from dormant latent conditions — useful, but with known limitations.
concepts.title: Swiss Cheese (Barrier) Model

concepts.description: Where a system's boundary is drawn is not a fact about the system but a choice tied to the observer's objective — so different legitimate observers of the same system see different systems, and each is blind to couplings the others can see.
concepts.title: System Boundaries Are Perspective-Dependent

concepts.description: Once a project's core technology matures past the point where incremental engineering can keep delivering gains, resilience requires an explicit, dedicated role responsible for the coherence of the whole system across technical, managerial, and institutional domains — a role no single discipline's expertise covers.
concepts.title: The System Integrator Role

concepts.description: Flexibility negotiated at the system level to keep an organisation viable can be delivered by transferring burden onto the individuals operating inside it, raising an open question resilience engineering has not settled: whether system-level and individual-level resilience reinforce each other or trade off.
concepts.title: System Resilience vs Individual Resilience — Competing or Converging?

concepts.description: Control-theoretic models (Leveson's STAMP, Perrow) treat safety as an emergent property of the whole system and accidents as erosion of control over component interactions, not as component failures.
concepts.title: Systems-Theoretic Accident Model

concepts.description: A field-derived taxonomy of the individual and team cognitive strategies air traffic controllers actually use during emergencies — and the finding that standard simulator refresher training scores well on every strategy while real incidents fail specifically at error management and workload redistribution, the two strategies standardised training never exercises.
concepts.title: T2EAM: Taskwork and Teamwork Strategies for Resilient Performance

concepts.description: As successive layers of defence-in-depth are breached, a system moves through normal, abnormal, and emergency operating envelopes in sequence — each breach a deliberate lowering of expectations, not a single jump from safe to unsafe.
concepts.title: Tactical Retreat Through Defence Layers

concepts.description: Safety-relevant information can be known by an individual team member yet never surface into the team's shared, spoken understanding — a distinct failure mode from nobody knowing and from nobody hearing.
concepts.title: Team Preconscious Knowledge

concepts.description: A framework, developed from Line Operations Safety Audit data, that treats errors and deviations as routinely embedded in normal practice — defining professionalism as managing context and recovering performance within acceptable boundaries, not as avoiding error altogether.
concepts.title: Threat and Error Management (TEM)

concepts.description: Effective learning requires frequent opportunities, cases similar enough to generalise across, and a chance to verify the lesson before it matters — accidents in safe systems structurally fail all three, which is why learning from everyday normal work outperforms learning from accidents.
concepts.title: Three Conditions for Effective Learning

concepts.description: Systemic and knowledge deficiencies that surface as an operational failure were usually built in far earlier, across three distinct engineering design phases — so an investigation confined to the moment of failure misses where the fix actually belongs.
concepts.title: Three Design Phases Where Resilience Deficiencies Originate

concepts.description: Managerial resilience's non-technical skills can be formally trained by importing practices from other high-risk operational domains, but training alone fails without an organisational culture that rewards the upward challenge it teaches.
concepts.title: Training Managerial Resilience Skills

concepts.description: Routine work stays at the concrete, low-abstraction level of Rasmussen's goal-means hierarchy where goals rarely conflict; a resilient response to sudden demand requires traversing upward to resolve conflicts, deliberately sacrificing lower-level goals to preserve the system's top-level viability.
concepts.title: Traversing the Goal-Means Hierarchy Under Resilient Performance

concepts.description: Reason's Tripod method for proactively auditing the latent organisational conditions that generate accidents — targeting the one part of the accident-causation chain that is actually predictable and controllable before an event happens.
concepts.title: Tripod Basic Risk Factors

concepts.description: A bias label that could equally have been applied had the opposite outcome occurred explains nothing about the actual decision — it only redescribes a bad outcome in psychological-sounding language.
concepts.title: Unfalsifiable Bias Attribution

concepts.description: Brian Wynne's term for the gap between a technology's tidy engineering image and its messy, not-fully-governable behaviour in real operational practice, and the specific conditions under which people reinterpret anomalous data rather than revise their beliefs about it.
concepts.title: Unruly Technology

concepts.description: Resilience is a cross-scale process — macro-level goal-setting and intent ("downward") meeting frontline craftsmanship and improvisation ("upward") — and it fails when either direction is missing, not just when one is.
concepts.title: Upward and Downward Resilience

concepts.description: Zero-harm targets demand that management manipulate an outcome metric rather than the systemic inputs that produce it, driving data falsification, moral stigmatisation, and misallocated investigation effort.
concepts.title: Vision Zero and the Dependent-Variable Error

concepts.description: Reported incidents are like bullet holes on returning bombers — markers of survivable damage — while catastrophic vulnerability hides in normal work that never generates a report.
concepts.title: Wald's Bomber Paradox

concepts.description: Resilience shows up as three distinct capabilities relative to when a threat occurs — foreseeing and avoiding it, coping while it unfolds, and repairing after it — and possessing one does not guarantee the others.
concepts.title: Westrum's Three Temporal Horizons of Resilience

concepts.description: Pathological, bureaucratic, and generative cultures differ in how information flows — and information flow is what determines safety, resilience, and performance in complex sociotechnical systems.
concepts.title: Westrum's Typology of Organizational Culture

concepts.description: Seven reasons an organisational focus on human error — error counts, error rates, error eradication targets — systematically misleads safety management.
concepts.title: Why Counting and Targeting 'Human Error' Misleads

concepts.description: The inevitable gap between how work is specified in rules and procedures and how it must actually be performed under real conditions — the gap where both resilience and drift live.
concepts.title: Work-as-Imagined vs Work-as-Done

concepts.description: Units or echelons each making locally rational adjustments can collectively undermine the whole system, the same dynamic as a tragedy of the commons with safety margin as the depleted shared resource.
concepts.title: Working at Cross-Purposes — Locally Adaptive, Globally Maladaptive
